overview.title: Padding in Keras, strides, and the start of max pooling
overview.main_topic: The Conv2D padding argument ("valid" vs "same"), strided convolutions as a second way output size changes, and the introduction of max pooling as the usual downsampling tool in classification models.
overview.central_idea: padding="valid" (default) means no padding while "same" preserves width and height; the stride is the distance between successive windows (default 1), and stride 2 halves width and height. Classification ConvNets usually downsample with max pooling instead, which halved 26 × 26 to 13 × 13 in the MNIST model.
overview.importance: Completes the set of knobs that determine a conv layer's output shape and motivates max pooling, whose purpose (aggressive downsampling) is analysed on the next page.
learning_objectives: Use the Conv2D padding argument and know its default.
Read figure 8.7 and compute the output size for a 3 × 3, stride-2 convolution on a 5 × 5 input.
Explain that stride 2 downsamples by a factor of 2 in addition to border effects.
State the role of max pooling: aggressive downsampling, e.g. 26 × 26 -> 13 × 13.
prerequisites: The MNIST ConvNet and its summary (p.256-257)

summary:
**Padding in Keras.** `Conv2D` exposes padding through the `padding` argument with two values: `"valid"`, no padding (only valid window locations are used), and `"same"`, "pad in such a way as to have an output with the same width and height as the input." The default is `"valid"`, which is why the MNIST model's convolutions shrink their inputs by two tiles.

**Strides.** So far the window centres were assumed contiguous. The distance between two successive windows is a parameter called the **stride**, default 1. Convolutions with stride greater than 1 are *strided convolutions*. Figure 8.7 shows a 3 × 3 convolution with stride 2 on a 5 × 5 input without padding: only four patches are extracted, centred on the tiles labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 (the corners of the central 3 × 3 region), giving a 2 × 2 output. Stride 2 downsamples width and height by a factor of 2, in addition to any border effects. Strided convolutions are rarely used in classification models but are handy for some model types, as the next chapter shows.

**Max pooling instead.** Classification models typically downsample with the **max-pooling** operation, already used in the first ConvNet example.

**8.1.2 The max-pooling operation.** In the MNIST ConvNet the feature-map size is halved after each `MaxPooling2D` layer: 26 × 26 before the first one, 13 × 13 after. That is max pooling's role: to aggressively downsample feature maps, much like strided convolutions. How it works and why downsampling is needed follow on p.264.

concepts.name: Padding argument (valid / same)
concepts.definition: Conv2D's padding argument: "valid" = no padding, "same" = pad so output width and height equal the input's; default "valid".
concepts.intuition: Choose whether the conv is allowed to shrink the map.
concepts.technical: With stride 1, "valid" gives n − k + 1, "same" gives n. With stride s, "same" gives ⌈n/s⌉.
concepts.misconception: "same" does not mean the depth stays the same; depth is always the number of filters.

concepts.name: Stride
concepts.definition: The distance between two successive convolution windows; default 1.
concepts.intuition: How many tiles the window jumps each step.
concepts.technical: Output size $\lfloor (n + 2p - k)/s \rfloor + 1$. Stride 2 halves width and height (plus border effects).
concepts.significance: A way to downsample inside a conv layer; rare in classification models, used in some other architectures.
concepts.misconception: Stride does not change the window size or the number of parameters.

concepts.name: Max pooling (role)
concepts.definition: An operation that aggressively downsamples feature maps, much like strided convolutions; halves 26 × 26 to 13 × 13 in the MNIST model.
concepts.intuition: Keep the strongest response in each small block.
concepts.technical: Usually 2 × 2 windows with stride 2, taking the max per channel (detailed on p.264). No trainable parameters (0 params in the summary, p.257).
concepts.significance: The standard downsampling choice in classification ConvNets.
concepts.misconception: Max pooling does not change the number of channels.

concepts.name: Downsampling
concepts.definition: Reducing the height and width of feature maps.
concepts.technical: Achieved with strided convolutions or pooling.
concepts.significance: Keeps feature maps manageable and builds spatial hierarchies (p.265).
concepts.example: Stride 2 or 2 × 2 max pooling both halve resolution.
concepts.misconception: Downsampling is not only a speed trick; it is what lets later layers see larger windows of the input.

math.title: Output size with stride
math.source_text: In figure 8.7, you can see the patches extracted by a 3 × 3 convolution with stride 2 over a 5 × 5 input (without padding) ... Using stride 2 means the width and height of the feature map are downsampled by a factor of 2 (in addition to any changes induced by border effects).
math.operations: Count window starting positions spaced s apart that fit within the (padded) input.
math.purpose: Combines border effects (p.262) and strides into one rule; the book states it in words.
math.interpretation: Stride divides the number of positions by s; the −k term is the border effect.
math.intuition: How many hops of size s fit after placing the first window.
math.numerical_example: Figure 8.7: $\lfloor (5 - 3)/2 \rfloor + 1 = 2$, a 2 × 2 output (4 patches). Valid stride-2 conv on 28 × 28: $\lfloor 25/2 \rfloor + 1 = 13$. Stride 1: $5-3+1 = 3$ (figure 8.5).

math.title: 2 × 2 max pooling halves size
math.source_text: before the first MaxPooling2D layers, the feature map is 26 × 26, but the max-pooling operation halves it to 13 × 13

variables.meaning: Feature-map height or width before pooling

math.operations: Same formula as m1 with k = 2, s = 2, p = 0.
math.purpose: Explains the halving the authors point out.
math.interpretation: Each 2 × 2 block becomes one value; an odd leftover row/column is dropped.

deeper.title: Shapes under the four combinations
deeper.body:
Beyond the book: Conv2D with a 3 × 3 window on a 28 × 28 input:

| padding | strides | output |
|---|---|---|
| "valid" | 1 | 26 × 26 |
| "same" | 1 | 28 × 28 |
| "valid" | 2 | 13 × 13 |
| "same" | 2 | 14 × 14 |

The last two illustrate the book's phrase "downsampled by a factor of 2 (in addition to any changes induced by border effects)."

deeper.title: Verify in Keras
deeper.body:
Beyond the book:

```python
import keras
from keras import layers
x = keras.Input(shape=(5, 5, 1))
print(layers.Conv2D(1, 3, strides=2)(x).shape)   # (None, 2, 2, 1)  figure 8.7
x = keras.Input(shape=(26, 26, 64))
print(layers.MaxPooling2D(2)(x).shape)          # (None, 13, 13, 64)
```

deeper.title: Strided convolution vs max pooling
deeper.body: Both downsample by 2. A strided conv learns *how* to summarize each region (its kernel is trained) but evaluates only every other position, so it may skip over a strongly responding location. Max pooling (after a stride-1 conv) computes features at every position and then keeps the strongest response in each block. The book notes the latter is the usual choice in classification models; p.264-265 explain the reasons for downsampling at all. (The comparison is our explanation, not the book's.)

misconceptions.claim: Conv2D pads by default to keep the image size.
misconceptions.correction: The default is padding="valid", i.e. no padding.

misconceptions.claim: padding="same" keeps the output size equal to the input even with stride 2.
misconceptions.correction: The "same" definition in the book refers to keeping width and height; with stride 2 the output is still downsampled by 2 (⌈n/2⌉).

misconceptions.claim: Strided convolutions are the standard way to downsample in classification ConvNets.
misconceptions.correction: The book says they are rarely used in classification models; max pooling is the usual choice there.

misconceptions.claim: Max pooling halves the number of channels.
misconceptions.correction: It halves height and width; channels are unchanged (26 × 26 × 64 -> 13 × 13 × 64).

takeaways: Conv2D padding: "valid" (no padding, the default) or "same" (output width and height equal the input's).
Stride = distance between successive windows; default 1; stride > 1 gives strided convolutions.
Figure 8.7: 3 × 3, stride 2 on 5 × 5 without padding extracts 4 patches (2 × 2 output).
Stride 2 downsamples width and height by 2, in addition to border effects.
Classification models usually downsample with max pooling, not strides; MaxPooling2D halved 26 × 26 to 13 × 13.

questions.question: What is the default value of Conv2D's padding argument?
questions.explanation: The page states the default is "valid" (no padding). "same" must be requested explicitly; "causal" and "full" are not the Conv2D default.

questions.question: A 3 × 3 convolution with stride 2 and no padding is applied to a 5 × 5 input (figure 8.7). How many patches are extracted and what is the output size? What about a 7 × 7 input?
questions.answer: 4 patches, 2 × 2 output; for 7 × 7: ⌊(7 − 3)/2⌋ + 1 = 3, a 3 × 3 output (9 patches).
questions.explanation: Valid centres are the interior tiles; stride 2 keeps every other one.

questions.question: What is a stride?
questions.answer: The distance between two successive convolution windows; it defaults to 1.
questions.explanation: Defined in the 'Understanding convolution strides' paragraph.

questions.question: What does the book mean by 'downsampled by a factor of 2 (in addition to any changes induced by border effects)'? Give the output size of a 3 × 3 stride-2 convolution on 28 × 28 with "valid" and with "same" padding.
questions.answer: Stride halves the size, and valid padding additionally loses border tiles: "valid" gives 13 × 13, "same" gives 14 × 14.

questions.question: According to the page, which operation do classification models tend to use to downsample feature maps?
options: Global average pooling at every layer
questions.explanation: The book says strided convolutions are rarely used in classification models; instead max pooling is used. Padding doesn't downsample, and global average pooling is used once at the end (p.258).

questions.question: In the MNIST ConvNet, the second MaxPooling2D receives an 11 × 11 map. What does it output, and why not 5.5 × 5.5 or 6 × 6?
questions.answer: 5 × 5: with 2 × 2 windows and stride 2 only 5 full windows fit along each axis; the last row/column is dropped.
questions.explanation: Pooling uses valid windows by default, so the size is floored (⌊11/2⌋ = 5), as shown in the summary on p.257.

questions.question: Can you explain, for each layer of the MNIST model, which of the three effects (border effect, stride, pooling) changes its spatial size?
questions.answer: Conv layers: border effect only (valid padding, stride 1): −2. Pooling layers: halving. Strides are not used.
questions.explanation: If you can produce 28→26→13→11→5→3 from these rules, you've mastered pages 262-263.
